title: Naso: the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26)
hook: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee", still said over children and congregations
tomorrow: Naso: the same gift twelve times (Numbers 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nazir, and your line, a vow for a season. How's the first day without the thing you gave up? Today, three lines from this book that are still said aloud every week. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

Friday night, in a lot of Jewish homes, before the meal. A parent puts both hands on a child's head. The child might be four and wriggling, or seventeen and rolling their eyes, or thirty and home for the weekend. The parent says a few quiet words, the same words every week. In a synagogue in Jerusalem, every morning, a row of men with prayer shawls over their heads lift their hands toward the congregation and chant the very same words. The words come from today's portion. They're three lines long.
screen: `HANDS ON A CHILD'S HEAD.` → `A ROW OF RAISED HANDS.` → `THE SAME THREE LINES.`

segments.voice: God tells Moses to give Aaron and his sons these words for blessing the people. "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." In Hebrew it's called Birkat Kohanim, the blessing of the priests. Count the Hebrew words and they grow: three in the first line, five in the second, seven in the third. Like a breath getting deeper. The first line asks for blessing and protection: the things that keep a life safe. The second asks for God's face to shine: warmth, favor, grace. The third asks God to lift up a face toward you, the same root as naso, lift, and ends with shalom, peace. Then, right after the three lines, the Torah adds that the priests shall put God's name upon the people, and God will bless them. The priests speak, but it is God who blesses. The kohanim are a channel, not the source. Today, descendants of Aaron, kohanim, still say it. In Israel it's said every day; in many synagogues outside Israel, on festivals. They raise their hands with fingers spread, prayer shawls over their heads, and the congregation lowers its eyes. At home, on Friday night, parents say it over their children. The words are old outside the Bible, too. In 1979, archaeologists near Jerusalem found two tiny silver scrolls, rolled up like amulets, centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls. Inscribed on them: a version of this blessing.
screen: `BLESS, SHINE, LIFT, PEACE.` · `THREE, FIVE, SEVEN WORDS.` · `THE PRIESTS SPEAK. GOD BLESSES.` · `TWO SILVER SCROLLS.` · then, large: `THE LORD BLESS THEE, AND KEEP THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless someone with these words. Breathe, and bring one person to mind: a child, a friend, a parent, someone far away, someone struggling. Picture their face. If these words fit your life, say the three lines silently toward that person, slowly, one line per breath, and let each line grow a little longer, the way the Hebrew does. If they don't fit, simply hold the person in mind and wish them safety, warmth and peace. The bell holds the time.
Birkat Kohanim. The priestly blessing: three lines that grow from three words to seven, ending in peace.
Your line: bless thee, and keep thee. Today, tell the person you pictured one sentence of good you wish them, plainly, out loud or in writing. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice old blessing from the Bible.
what it means: a blessing still chanted by Aaron's descendants and said by parents over children every week.
what a scholar hears: silver amulets from Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem carry a version of it, among the oldest known fragments of biblical text.

notes: Numbers 6:24–26 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; confirm punctuation and capitalization.
Ketef Hinnom: found 1979, usually dated to around the late 7th or early 6th century BCE, 'centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls'. Confirm.
Customs for when the blessing is chanted (daily in Israel; festivals in many diaspora Ashkenazi communities; daily in many Sephardic ones) and the Friday-night parental blessing: confirm phrasing.
The practice invites the listener to say the verses only 'if these words fit your life'; no new prayer is written.

Audit (second sample): removed stock lines ('a line people often miss', 'one more thing a curious person would repeat', 'the biggest word of all') and the unsourced superlative 'maybe the most spoken verses in this whole book'; the priests-speak-God-blesses point is now tied to Numbers 6:27, paraphrased.
